chapter.name: Probability
chapter.blurb: This chapter treats an event as a subset of the sample space, classifies events (impossible, sure, simple, compound), combines them with 'not', 'or', 'and' and 'but not', and tests whether events are mutually exclusive and exhaustive. It then introduces the axiomatic approach to probability, the formula for equally likely outcomes, the addition rule P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B) and the complement rule P(not A) = 1 - P(A).

scope_in.item: Define an event as any subset of the sample space and write the subset for an event described in words (coins tossed two or three times, one die, two dice as 36 ordered pairs), including 'exactly', 'at least' and 'at most' descriptions
Decide whether an event has occurred for a given outcome (the outcome belongs to the event)

Classify events as impossible (phi), sure (S), simple or elementary (one sample point) and compound (more than one sample point), and use the fact that n distinct sample points give exactly n simple events

Form the complementary event 'not A' = A' = S - A and the events 'A or B' (union), 'A and B' (intersection) and 'A but not B' = A - B = A and B', and list them for dice, coin and numbered-card experiments
Decide whether two events are mutually exclusive (cannot occur simultaneously, 'A and B' = phi), knowing that simple events are always mutually exclusive
Decide whether events are exhaustive (their union is S, so at least one necessarily occurs) and whether a set of events is mutually exclusive and exhaustive
State the three axioms of probability (P(E) >= 0, P(S) = 1, P(E or F) = P(E) + P(F) for mutually exclusive E and F), deduce P(phi) = 0, and know that P is a function from the power set of S to [0, 1]

Check whether an assignment of probabilities to the outcomes of a finite sample space is valid (each between 0 and 1, sum equal to 1), including assignments in which the outcomes are not equally likely
Find P(A) as the sum of the probabilities of the sample points in A for a given assignment
Use P(E) = n(E)/n(S) when outcomes are equally likely: coins, dice, a deck of 52 cards, discs or balls in a bag, letters of a word, people selected at random

Find probabilities by counting arrangements with n! or P(n, r) and selections with C(n, r), as in the chapter's examples on committees, hands of cards, orders of visiting cities and finishing orders in a race

Use the addition rule P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B), follow its derivation from axiom (iii), and use it to find any one of the four probabilities from the other three or to test whether given probabilities are consistently defined
Use P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) for mutually exclusive events, and P(A but not B) = P(A) - P(A and B) for 'only one' problems
Use the complement rule P(not A) = 1 - P(A), with De Morgan's law for 'neither A nor B' = 'not (A or B)' and with 'at least one' = 1 - P(none)
Know the result P(A or B or C) = P(A) + P(B) + P(C) - P(A and B) - P(A and C) - P(B and C) + P(A and B and C) proved in Example 11

concepts.name: Events and types of events
concepts.description: An event as a subset of the sample space, when an event is said to occur, and the impossible, sure, simple and compound events.
concepts.idea: Every question about an experiment is a question about some set of outcomes, so an event is simply a subset of the sample space.
concepts.rule: Any subset E of a sample space S is an event. E has occurred if the outcome of the experiment belongs to E. The empty set phi is the impossible event and S is the sure event. An event with only one sample point is a simple (elementary) event; an event with more than one sample point is a compound event. A sample space with n distinct elements has exactly n simple events.
concepts.example: Tossing a coin twice, S = {HH, HT, TH, TT}: 'exactly one head' is the compound event {HT, TH}, 'exactly two tails' is the simple event {TT}, and 'more than two tails' is phi.

questions.q: A coin is tossed three times. Consider the events E: 'exactly one head appears', F: 'at least one head appears' and G: 'at most one head appears'. Write the three subsets. Then identify the sample points that are in F but not in E, and those that are in G but not in E, and use them to explain how 'at least one' and 'at most one' differ from 'exactly one'.
questions.a: E = {HTT, THT, TTH}. F = {HTT, THT, TTH, HHT, HTH, THH, HHH}. G = {TTT, HTT, THT, TTH}. The points in F but not in E are HHT, HTH, THH and HHH: 'at least one head' also allows two or three heads. The only point in G but not in E is TTT: 'at most one head' also allows no head at all. So E is a subset of both F and G; 'at least one' adds the outcomes with more heads and 'at most one' adds the outcome with fewer heads.

questions.a: Sample answer. Impossible: 'a number greater than 6 appears' = phi, since no outcome satisfies it. Sure: 'a number less than 7 appears' = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} = S, since every outcome satisfies it. Simple: 'the number 5 appears' = {5}, which has only one sample point. concepts.name: Algebra of events
concepts.description: Combining events with set operations: the complementary event 'not A', and the events 'A or B', 'A and B' and 'A but not B'.
concepts.idea: Events are sets, so new events are built from old ones with complement, union, intersection and difference.
concepts.rule: 'not A' = A' = S - A (the complementary event). 'A or B' is the union of A and B (either A or B or both). 'A and B' is the intersection of A and B. 'A but not B' = A - B, which is the same as 'A and B''.
concepts.example: Rolling a die with A = 'a prime number' = {2, 3, 5} and B = 'an odd number' = {1, 3, 5}: 'A or B' = {1, 2, 3, 5}, 'A and B' = {3, 5}, 'A but not B' = {2}, 'not A' = {1, 4, 6}.

concepts.name: Mutually exclusive and exhaustive events
concepts.description: Deciding whether events are mutually exclusive (disjoint), exhaustive (their union is S), both or neither.
concepts.idea: Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together; exhaustive events leave no outcome uncovered. The two properties are separate and must be tested separately.
concepts.rule: A and B are mutually exclusive if they cannot occur simultaneously, i.e. 'A and B' = phi. Events E1, E2, ..., En are exhaustive if their union is S, i.e. at least one of them necessarily occurs whenever the experiment is performed. If in addition they are pairwise disjoint they are mutually exclusive and exhaustive. Simple events of a sample space are always mutually exclusive.
concepts.example: Tossing a coin three times: A = 'no head' = {TTT}, B = 'exactly one head' = {HTT, THT, TTH}, C = 'at least two heads' = {HHT, HTH, THH, HHH} are pairwise disjoint and their union is S, so they are mutually exclusive and exhaustive.

questions.a: A = {1, 2}, B = {3, 6}, C = {4, 5}. No two of these sets have a common element, so the events are pairwise disjoint, i.e. mutually exclusive. Their union is {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} = S, so they are exhaustive. Hence A, B and C are mutually exclusive and exhaustive.

questions.q: Two dice are thrown. A is the event 'an even number appears on the first die', B is 'an odd number appears on the first die' and C is 'the sum of the numbers on the dice is at most 5'. State whether each statement is true or false, with a reason: (i) A = B', (ii) A and B' are mutually exclusive, (iii) A', B' and C are mutually exclusive and exhaustive.
questions.a: (i) True: the first die shows either an even or an odd number, so the outcomes not in B are exactly those in A. (ii) False: B' = A, so 'A and B'' = A, which is not phi. (iii) False: A' = B and B' = A, and C has outcomes in common with both, for example (1, 1) is in both B and C and (2, 1) is in both A and C, so the three events are not mutually exclusive (although their union is S).
s: (i) True, with the reason that A consists of exactly the outcomes not in B
(ii) False, because B' = A and so their intersection is A, not phi
(iii) False, with an outcome such as (1, 1) or (2, 1) shown to be common to C and one of A', B'

questions.a: A = {2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12}, B = {3, 6, 9, 12}, C = {1, 5, 7, 11}. (i) The union of A, B and C is {1, 2, ..., 12} = S, so they are exhaustive. (ii) 'A and B' = {6, 12}, which is not phi, so they are not mutually exclusive (C is disjoint from both A and B). Changing B to 'the number is an odd multiple of 3' = {3, 9} removes the overlap with A and still leaves the union equal to S, so A, the new B and C are mutually exclusive and exhaustive.

Finds 'A and B' = {6, 12}, so the events are not mutually exclusive

questions.q: A coin is tossed twice. Sara claims that the events 'at least one head appears' and 'at least one tail appears' are mutually exclusive and exhaustive, because between them they cover every outcome. Evaluate her claim.
questions.a: Sara is only half right. 'At least one head' = {HH, HT, TH} and 'at least one tail' = {HT, TH, TT}. Their union is {HH, HT, TH, TT} = S, so they are exhaustive. But HT and TH belong to both, so their intersection is not phi and they are not mutually exclusive. Covering every outcome shows only that events are exhaustive.

questions.a: Sample answer. (i) 'three heads' = {HHH} and 'three tails' = {TTT}: no common outcome, but their union is not S. (ii) 'no tail' = {HHH}, 'exactly one tail' = {HHT, HTH, THH} and 'at least two tails' = {HTT, THT, TTH, TTT}: pairwise disjoint with union S. (iii) 'at least two heads' = {HHH, HHT, HTH, THH} and 'the first coin shows a head' = {HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT}: HHH, HHT and HTH are common. Any correct events with subsets and reasons earn full marks.

concepts.name: Axiomatic approach and the probability of an event
concepts.description: The three axioms of probability, valid assignments of probabilities to outcomes, and P(A) as the sum of the probabilities of the sample points in A.
concepts.idea: Probability is a function on events that obeys three rules; any assignment of numbers to the outcomes that respects them is a valid probability model, whether or not the outcomes are equally likely.
concepts.rule: Axioms: (i) P(E) >= 0 for any event E, (ii) P(S) = 1, (iii) if E and F are mutually exclusive then P(E or F) = P(E) + P(F). It follows that P(phi) = 0. For S = {w1, w2, ..., wn}: 0 <= P(wi) <= 1 for each wi, P(w1) + P(w2) + ... + P(wn) = 1, and for any event A, P(A) is the sum of P(wi) over the sample points wi in A.
concepts.example: For a coin tossed twice with P(HH) = 1/4, P(HT) = 1/7, P(TH) = 2/7, P(TT) = 9/28 (a valid assignment), the event 'both tosses give the same result' = {HH, TT} has probability 1/4 + 9/28 = 4/7.

concepts.name: Probability with equally likely outcomes
concepts.description: Using P(E) = n(E)/n(S) for coins, dice, cards, letters, arrangements and selections counted with factorials and C(n, r).
concepts.idea: When every outcome has the same chance, finding a probability is a counting problem: count the favourable outcomes and divide by the total.
concepts.rule: If S has n equally likely outcomes, each has probability 1/n. If n(S) = n and n(E) = m, then P(E) = m/n = (number of outcomes favourable to E)/(total possible outcomes). The outcomes counted must themselves be equally likely: ordered pairs for two dice (36), ordered strings for coins, and C(n, r) selections or n! arrangements where the chapter's examples use them.
concepts.example: A committee of two is selected from two men and two women: P(one man) = C(2, 1) x C(2, 1) / C(4, 2) = 4/6 = 2/3.

concepts.name: Probability of the event 'A or B'
concepts.description: The addition rule P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B), its special case for mutually exclusive events, and its use to find any one of the four probabilities.
concepts.idea: Adding P(A) and P(B) counts the outcomes common to A and B twice, so their probability must be taken away once.

questions.a: Since A and 'B but not A' are mutually exclusive and their union is 'A or B', axiom (iii) gives P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B but not A) ... (1). Subtracting (2) from (1): P(A or B) - P(B) = P(A) - P(A and B). Hence P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B).

concepts.name: Probability of the event 'not A'
concepts.description: The complement rule P(not A) = 1 - P(A) and its use for 'not', 'neither ... nor' and 'at least one' probabilities.
concepts.idea: A and 'not A' between them cover the whole sample space without overlap, so their probabilities add up to 1; it is often easier to find the probability of what you do not want and subtract it from 1.
concepts.rule: A and A' are mutually exclusive and exhaustive, so by axioms (ii) and (iii) P(A) + P(A') = 1, i.e. P(not A) = 1 - P(A). By De Morgan's law 'not E and not F' = 'not (E or F)', so P(not E and not F) = 1 - P(E or F). P(at least one) = 1 - P(none).
concepts.example: One card is drawn from a well-shuffled deck of 52 cards: P(not an ace) = 1 - 4/52 = 12/13 and P(not a diamond) = 1 - 1/4 = 3/4.

questions.q: Two students Ravi and Sana appear in an examination. The probability that Ravi qualifies is 0.3, the probability that Sana qualifies is 0.5 and the probability that both qualify is 0.1. Find the probability that (a) neither of them qualifies, (b) at least one of them does not qualify, (c) only one of them qualifies.
questions.a: Let E and F be the events that Ravi and Sana qualify. P(E or F) = 0.3 + 0.5 - 0.1 = 0.7. (a) 'Neither qualifies' is 'not E and not F' = 'not (E or F)' by De Morgan's law, so its probability is 1 - 0.7 = 0.3. (b) 'At least one does not qualify' is the complement of 'both qualify', so its probability is 1 - 0.1 = 0.9. (c) 'Only one qualifies' is 'E but not F' or 'F but not E', which are mutually exclusive, so its probability is (0.3 - 0.1) + (0.5 - 0.1) = 0.6.
s: (a) P(E or F) = 0.7 and P(neither) = 1 - 0.7 = 0.3

questions.q: A fair coin is tossed twice. Dev says that P(at least one head) = 1 - P(at least one tail), because heads and tails are opposites. Evaluate his statement.
questions.a: Dev is wrong. The complement of 'at least one head' = {HH, HT, TH} is 'no head' = {TT}, not 'at least one tail' = {HT, TH, TT}; the outcomes HT and TH lie in both of his events, so they are not complementary. Correctly, P(at least one head) = 1 - P(no head) = 1 - 1/4 = 3/4, whereas his rule gives 1 - 3/4 = 1/4.
s: Shows that the complement of 'at least one head' is 'no head' = {TT}, not 'at least one tail'
Gives the correct value 1 - 1/4 = 3/4

questions.a: Sample answer. 'A bag contains 5 white and 3 black balls. Two balls are drawn at random together. Find the probability that at least one is black.' Solution: two balls can be chosen in C(8, 2) = 28 equally likely ways. The complement of 'at least one black' is 'both white', which can happen in C(5, 2) = 10 ways, so P(both white) = 10/28 = 5/14.
